title: Pork chop, coated, lean and fat, edible

content.title: About
content.content: Coated pork chops can include both lean and fattier cuts of meat. The coating is usually a mixture of flour, egg and breadcrumbs, giving the dish a crunchy crust. These chops are commonly pan‑fried or baked and are a popular dish in many cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats globally.
The coating helps retain juices inside the meat, making it more tender.
In Russia, coated pork chops are traditionally served with mashed potatoes or buckwheat.
Japan’s version, tonkatsu, is a breaded pork cutlet served with tonkatsu sauce.
Fattier pork contains more vitamin B12 and iron than lean cuts.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is high in thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc and phosphorus in pork contribute to healthy blood and bones.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Fattier portions contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat provides lasting fullness.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts may raise cholesterol levels if eaten frequently.

items.title: Foodborne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor parasites such as Trichinella.

items.title: Allergy to coating ingredients
items.content: Some people may react to wheat, eggs or dairy used in the breading.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared breaded products often contain added salt, which should be considered for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dredge the chops in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, then fry until golden or bake at 200 °C for 20‑25 minutes. Serve hot with vegetables, potatoes or a salad. A squeeze of lemon or a mustard‑based sauce adds extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh pork should be kept in the refrigerator at +2‑+4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. Frozen pork lasts up to 6 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking. Cooked breaded chops are best consumed within 1‑2 days, stored in an airtight container.
